updates/2026-09-18.1---a-mixed-bag-sort-.title: 2026-09-18.1 - A Mixed Bag Sort of Day
updates/2026-09-18.1---a-mixed-bag-sort-.content:
Some days are not about getting one larger thing done, but many smaller things that we have been putting off for awhile. Also some days we just need to be thankful we did anything at all!
Bass VI Setup

I have been meaning to setup my new Bass VI, (in antigua finish ou la laa), but that would require actually taking the old factory strings off, and replacing them with the extra fan-say La Bella strings. Flatwounds, oh yah. This should give the bass a new and different sound, so I am anxious to hear it, but also anxious of wasting 60$ on string I may just hate.
Also, there is some quirks with this style of instrument produced by Fender and Squire. The bridge can rock back and forth and putting new strings on and ensuring the tuning is correct can be difficult when setup this way. A nice little hack is to throw these brass ferrules in the bridge post holes, the inside and outside diameters are a perfect fit and the bridge should stay in tune way better.

And what do you know? It does! that was worth about 15 cents and my time. But the string? That’s another story.
You know, I don’t hate them, I also don’t think I love them. They are their own thing, they do in fact have a distinct and i would call muted sound. It sounds interesting distorted but the true beauty comes in on clean. The Bass sings, the notes are so clear and clean, this is where the world of difference is. Playing something like Hey You but Pink Floyd, the strings really do the heavy lifting for the song. I do like this tone, it’s not an all use case sort of thing, but I see the appeal. If the Bass VI was fretless, then I think this would be a no brainer… and maybe that’s an idea for the future.

I did not intonate of adjust the truss rod, the bass was playing so well and the action felt good, so i left it as is. Later I will install strap locks so the strap does never comes off accidentally and send my precious, hideous bass flying into harms way or left solely to the whims of gravity.
Oh, Penny. Why that name for a bass? Well, all instruments need a name. To me, it kind of looks like a moldy Piece of Bread? Work with me here, so Penny is short for Penicillin? Dad joke levels of bad. Go ahead, groan, I’ll wait.
One observation I had was the tuners are still shit. I don’t find them to be this bass on my other Squire Bass VI, so that’s a little disappointing. I think in the near future I will replace the tuners will better quality ones, but that is a project for another day…
GitHub Page
This one does not need an essay write up. My GitHub landing page was a little too simple and lack luster, I wanted to put more about me and infect it with my personality so I did. I have grown since I wrote that landing and most of that code in my repo, and with me starting to archive projects more religiously this seemed like a good time for it.
It’s quite possible I will change the landing a few times, and that it will be totally different in a few years time, so until then and until that update let me just post al ink to what it looks like now.
GitHub Landing 9-18-2026

updates/2026-09-18.2---i-made-my-midi-dr.filePath: Updates/2026-09-18.2 - I Made My MIDI Drummer Worse on Purpose.md
updates/2026-09-18.2---i-made-my-midi-dr.title: 2026-09-18.2 - I Made My MIDI Drummer Worse on Purpose
updates/2026-09-18.2---i-made-my-midi-dr.content:
I write a lot of my drum parts in Guitar Pro, I’m not saying it’s the best, but when you’ve used something for 25+ years and it just works it’s kind of hard to switch.
It is less great when I export the MIDI, drop it into REAPER, and discover that my drummer has apparently been replaced by a machine with atomic-clock timing and perfect control over every muscle in its body. I know metal drummers are precise but not everyone is Gene Hoglan.
Every hit is exactly where I told it to be, every note is perfectly obedient.
It sounds fake AF.
Obviously there are already ways to “humanize” MIDI. Move notes a little bit. Randomize the velocity. Make everything slightly wrong.
But that started bothering me too, because humans aren’t just random.
A drummer doesn’t have four identical sticks floating around the kit. They have two hands, two feet, a dominant side, a weaker side, and a limited number of limbs that can only be in so many places at once.
So I made a REAPER script that tries to make my fake drummer worse at drumming in a more realistic way.
The goal was pretty simple.
I wanted to export a finished drum part from Guitar Pro, bring it into REAPER, select the MIDI item, run one script, and have it come out sounding less like Guitar Pro.
Not random. Human.
The first part was figuring out what every MIDI note actually represented.
So I made a drum map:
[35] = "Kick Drum",
[38] = "Snare Drum",
[42] = "Closed Hi-Hat",
[49] = "Crash Cymbal",
[51] = "Ride Cymbal",
And so on.
Then I gave every drum piece a default limb.
[36] = "DF",  -- Dominant Foot
[38] = "DH",  -- Dominant Hand
[42] = "NDH", -- Non-Dominant Hand
[44] = "NDF", -- Non-Dominant Foot
That was the important part.
Instead of looking at a MIDI note and saying: “Move this somewhere around here.”
The script can look at it and say:
“This is a snare hit. That is probably the dominant hand.”
“This is a hi-hat. That is probably the other hand.”
“This is a kick. Foot.”
Now we’re cooking.
Once every note has a limb, the four limbs can have their own personalities.
In Configuration.lua I gave them separate strength values:
dominateHandStrength = 99
nondominateHandStrength = 91
dominateFootStrength = 93
nondominateFootStrength = 87
So the dominant hand is naturally stronger than the non-dominant hand.
The feet aren’t identical either.
Then they each get their own timing bias, plus a little random variation.
velocityRandomRange = 10
timingRandomRange = 2
That means the “humanization” isn’t just one random number being thrown at every note.
A snare hit and a hi-hat hit can drift differently because they came from different simulated limbs.
The same goes for velocity.
Which is a very complicated way of making a computer slightly worse.
Perfect.
There was another problem though.
What happens when the MIDI asks one hand to hit two things at the same time? Or three?
The script groups notes that occur together and tries to resolve limb conflicts.
If two notes both want the dominant hand, one of them can be reassigned to the non-dominant hand.
The same basic idea applies to the feet.
There is also logic for alternating limbs through sequences instead of having one imaginary arm perform an entire drum roll like a woodpecker.
That part made the whole thing feel much more interesting to me.
I wasn’t just adding noise anymore. I was starting to model a person.
A very simple person. With four limbs. Who lives inside REAPER.
The script also has a list of MIDI notes that I don’t want in a standard drum-kit part.
Things like bongos, agogos, claves, vibraslap, cowbells, metronome hits, and a bunch of other percussion are marked separately from the kit pieces I actually expect.
So while analyzing the MIDI it can flag things that don’t belong in the kind of drum track I’m trying to process.
The actual program ended up split into a few modules:
Main.lua
Init.lua
Mapping.lua
AnalyzeMidi.lua
ProcessMidi.lua
Main.lua is basically the conductor.
It initializes the script, loads the mappings, analyzes the MIDI, and then processes it.
AnalyzeMidi.lua is where the interesting drummer-brain stuff happens.
It reads the MIDI notes, assigns limbs, groups simultaneous hits, alternates limbs where appropriate, checks for conflicts, and builds an internal representation of the performance.
Then ProcessMidi.lua takes that information and actually changes the MIDI.
Velocity gets adjusted around the configured strength for the limb.
Timing gets shifted according to that limb’s bias plus some randomness.
Then the original MIDI notes are replaced with the processed ones.
And REAPER says:
Humanization Complete!
I also apparently started making a GUI for this.
But that’s a project for another day. Maybe.
The current version in the repository is 0.9, which feels appropriate because there are definitely still rough edges.
There are checks I would tighten up.
The configuration could be much friendlier.
The GUI obviously went wherever unfinished GUIs go to die.
And there is a lot more that could theoretically be modeled if I ever wanted to get ridiculous with it.
Tempo.
Fatigue.
Accents.
Ghost notes.
How far a hand has to move across the kit.
Different playing styles.
Different actual drummers.
That last one is probably the most interesting possibility.
The configuration is already structured around the idea of an emulated player’s timing and strength.
So instead of having one generic “humanize” button, there is at least the beginning of a system where different configurations could represent different feels.
Not random imperfection.
Specific imperfection.
Which I think is the thing I like most about this project.
Computers are extremely good at doing exactly what you tell them.
Music often sounds better when they don’t.
REAPER Drum Humanizer

updates/2026-09-19.1---my-mini-retro-tel.filePath: Updates/2026-09-19.1 - My Mini Retro Television Channels.md
updates/2026-09-19.1---my-mini-retro-tel.title: 2026-09-19.1 - My Mini Retro Television Channels
updates/2026-09-19.1---my-mini-retro-tel.content:
I Turned A Tiny TV Into A Cartridge Console
I bought this little thing called a My Mini Retro Television.
It is exactly what it sounds like.

A tiny fake old television with a little screen, a speaker, some buttons, and a bunch of old videos loaded onto it.
You turn it on, it plays a little startup video, and then you can click through the videos like you are changing channels.
There is even a little static / channel-change animation between videos.
It is very stupid. I love it.
The first thing I did was plug it into my computer because obviously I needed to know what was actually going on inside it.
The internal storage showed up like a normal USB drive with a few gigabytes of videos on it.
There were also a bunch of weird tiny files like:
._VIDEODROME TV SPOT.mp4
._TWILIGHT ZONE MARATHON.mp4
._TONIGHT ON HBO 1990.mp4
They were only a few KB each and looked like broken videos.
Turns out those are just AppleDouble metadata files from a Mac.
So that mystery was solved pretty quickly.
The actual videos were normal MP4 files.
One file immediately stood out:
0 MY MINI RETRO TELEVISION.mp4
That was the startup video.
I pulled it off the TV and inspected it so I would have a known-good format to work from.
It is:
H.264
618x480
30 FPS
yuv420p
AAC audio
44.1 kHz stereo
Which is incredibly useful because now I know exactly what this tiny little goblin television already likes.
So naturally the next question was:
Can I put my own videos on it?
Yes. Very yes.
I deleted the videos from the internal storage, backed everything up first because I am reckless but not stupid, and put Planet of the Apes on it. All of them. A whole galaxy of apes.
It played!
At this point I discovered something even better. The TV also supports USB flash drives.
This changed the entire project.
Instead of constantly replacing the internal storage, I could leave the TV basically stock and treat USB drives like cartridges.
Tiny TV cartridges.
I made a little diagnostic pack with four videos:
000 STARTUP SORT TEST.mp4
001 CHANNEL ONE.mp4
002 CHANNEL TWO.mp4
003 CHANNEL THREE.mp4
Each one had a giant number on screen and a different number of beeps so I could tell exactly what the TV was doing.
The first problem was immediately very 2026.
All the flash drives I could find were 64GB.
Windows will not normally let you format a 64GB drive as FAT32 through the regular format dialog.
Of course.
So I just threw the test files on it and plugged it intop the little TV anyways.
That worked perfectly. The TV saw the drive. The videos played. The audio worked. The files played sequentially. The numbering controlled the order.
Beautiful. So my problem, was not even a problem.
Then things got more interesting.
The TV behaves differently when it is playing from internal storage versus USB.
With the internal storage, I get:
startup video
video
channel-change static
video
channel-change static
...
power-off movie
With a USB drive inserted, I get:
startup video
"USB drive inserted"
USB video
USB video
USB video
...
No channel-change animation. No power-off movie.
And there is a hardware / firmware message on screen telling me the USB drive was inserted.
That message is now on my list.
I do not know if I can remove it. I do not know if I can change the text.
I definitely do not know if I can replace it with a tiny VHS cassette graphic.
But I have now ordered two more televisions as backups, so science may happen.
The USB discovery also gave me the dumbest and therefore best idea in the entire project. The flash drives should be physical media.
I bought twenty 4GB flash drives.

The idea is to make each one feel like a little cable TV cartridge.
Not twenty different shows.
Actual stations.
Things like:
NICK01
NICK02
NICK03
NICK04
SNICK
 
CN01
CN02
CN03
CN04
CN05
 
KWB01
KWB02
FOX96
BOOM01
BOOM02
 
POWER
SCIFI
UPN
HBO
AMC
So instead of putting one season of one show on a drive, I am building little fake broadcasts.
A Nickelodeon cart might have Rugrats, Hey Arnold!, CatDog, Doug, Angry Beavers, Rocko, etc.
A Cartoon Network cart might have Dexter’s Laboratory, The Powerpuff Girls, Ed, Edd n Eddy, Batman, Freakazoid, and Animaniacs.
The goal is not to make a “best of” playlist.
I want it to feel like I turned the TV on in 1999 and just started watching whatever happened to be on.
That meant I had to start researching what was actually syndicated and rerun heavily instead of just picking my favorite episodes.
Because if I am going to pretend this tiny plastic television is cable TV, apparently I am going to take that responsibility seriously.
I also dumped the contents of my TV library into a giant file list so I could start planning the carts around what I actually own.
There is a lot.
Nickelodeon.
Cartoon Network.
Kids’ WB.
Star Trek.
Voyager.
Tales from the Crypt.
Three Stooges.
Beast Wars.

It turns out I have accidentally been preparing for this project for years.
The next missing piece was commercials.
If the whole point is to make this feel like old television, then going:
Rugrats
Hey Arnold!
CatDog
Doug
is not enough.
It needs this:
Rugrats
1997 cereal commercial
Hey Arnold!
Nintendo commercial
CatDog
Pizza Hut commercial
Doug
PSA
Now we are getting somewhere.
I started looking for old commercial archives and found a few big collections.
Some have individually clipped commercials.
Some are giant VHS commercial-break dumps.
Some are old Nickelodeon, Cartoon Network, Kids’ WB, Fox Kids, Disney, HBO-ish late-night stuff, and general 90s television.
I am currently downloading several of those collections.
Some of the torrents are being annoying and hanging on missing files because apparently even my fake 90s cable system has infrastructure problems.
The plan is to build a large commercial library, hopefully around 120-150 clips, then split them into pools like:
KIDS_90S
KIDS_00S
GENERAL_90S
GENERAL_00S
LATE_NIGHT
PSA
Then each fake station cartridge can pull commercials from the appropriate pool.
I am also looking for old network IDs and bumpers.
The little clips that say things like:
You're watching Nickelodeon
We'll be right back
Now back to the show
Cartoon Network
Kids' WB
Those will make the cartridges feel much more like actual TV stations instead of folders full of videos.
Eventually I want each cart to start with a station ident, play a sequence of shows, drop in commercials between them, and maybe use fake static or tracking glitches to recreate the channel-change effect that USB mode loses.
There is also going to be a cart-builder script because I am absolutely not doing all of this manually twenty times.
The builder will eventually take:
a station
a list of shows
a commercial pool
some bumpers
a startup ident
and turn all of it into correctly numbered MP4 files encoded for the tiny television.
That part is still ahead of me.
Right now I have the television figured out enough to know this is actually going to work.
The USB cartridges work.
The playback order works.
The format works.
The station lineup exists.
The commercial archives are downloading.
And there are twenty tiny flash drives on the way to becoming the world’s least useful cable provider.
I also want to 3D print little VHS cassette cases for the flash drives. Maybe. Probably.
One thing at a time.

updates/2026-09-19.2---obsidian-vault,-w.filePath: Updates/2026-09-19.2 - Obsidian Vault, Wiki, or Blog. Yes.md
updates/2026-09-19.2---obsidian-vault,-w.title: Obsidian Vault, Wiki, or Blog? Yes.
updates/2026-09-19.2---obsidian-vault,-w.content:
Obsidian Vault, Wiki, or Blog? Yes.
I work on too much weird shit.
That is not a complaint.
The problem is that I finish something, move on to the next thing, and six months later I vaguely remember that I once spent three nights teaching a keyboard to type ‰ or stood up a game server or wrote some little utility that absolutely nobody asked for.
I wanted somewhere to keep all of that.
Discord felt too temporary and too closed off. Facebook, Twitter, YouTube, etc. sounded like turning my hobbies into Content™, which is not what I wanted either. A normal blog was closer, but I kept getting hung up on the same thing:
What happens when the blog platform goes away?
I don’t want my diary to belong to a website.
That was the useful realization.
The website should just be a view of the diary.
So I made an Obsidian vault called:
Shag's Lab

The actual vault lives on my PC at:
F:\[DIARY]\Shag's Lab

And the whole idea is basically summed up by the welcome page:

This is part blog, part wiki. All me.

There are really only two important concepts.
Updates are moments in time.
Projects are persistent things.
Updates are the chronological “here is what I have been doing” side of it. Projects are the “tell me everything about this particular rabbit hole” side.
A project gets its own folder, a Home note, Guides, Assets, whatever else it actually needs.
An update gets stupidly simple metadata:
---
type: update
date: 2026-09-19
project: Obsidian Vault to Website
publish: true
---
Project Home pages work similarly:
---
type: project
project: Obsidian Vault to Website
status: active
publish: true
---
The important property is:
publish: true

My vault can contain whatever I want.
The public website only gets the things I deliberately mark public.
That part mattered a lot.
Then I put the whole vault under Git.
Not the website.
The actual diary.
Every Markdown file, every guide, every project note, every original screenshot.
Now even if I rewrite a page five years from now, Git still has the old version.
That alone made this worth doing.
The next piece was Quartz.
Quartz takes Markdown and turns it into a static website, which is almost exactly what I wanted. I keep writing normal Obsidian notes and Quartz makes browser food out of them.
Of course it was not quite as simple as:
npm install happiness

There were a few adventures.
The folder name [DIARY] taught PowerShell that brackets are apparently exciting, so paths like this:
cd "F:\[DIARY]\Shag's Lab"
did not work the way I expected.
The answer was:
Set-Location -LiteralPath "F:\[DIARY]\Shag's Lab"
Then Quartz installed its default theme without actually installing its default theme.
So this:
Cannot find module '@quartz-themes/default'

was solved with:
npm install @quartz-themes/default
Then the homepage was called index.
Then it was a 404.
Then the Explorer was empty.
Then the graph was one lonely purple dot.
All completely reasonable once I realized Quartz had only been given one file.
Eventually I stopped manually copying things around and wrote a publisher.
That is where the setup became actually useful.
My normal source remains:
F:\[DIARY]\Shag's Lab

Quartz itself lives separately at:
F:\[DIARY]\ShagsLab-Web

The publisher scans the vault, regenerates Updates Home and Projects Home, collects only notes with publish: true, grabs the assets those notes actually use, maps Welcome.md to the website homepage, and feeds that sanitized copy to Quartz.
Then Quartz builds the finished static site.
The finished site is copied back into the same Git repository under:
.site\public

So there is only one repository.
Thank Christ.
The private GitHub repository contains both my permanent vault and a generated copy of the public website.
That also gives me an off-machine backup.
The web server is another Windows PC entirely.
It pulls the same private repo into:
C:\PGN\ShagsLab

Then a tiny BAT file copies only:
C:\PGN\ShagsLab\.site\public

into Apache’s actual public directory:
C:\xampp\htdocs\helvete\lab

That separation means the server can have the full private repo checked out without Apache exposing the vault itself.
Only the generated public site gets copied into the web root.
So publishing now looks like this:
HOME PC
 
Obsidian
   ↓
Publish-ShagsLab-HomePC.bat
   ↓
generate indexes
   ↓
filter public notes
   ↓
build Quartz
   ↓
.site\public
   ↓
Git commit + push
   ↓
GitHub
 
 
WEB HOST
 
Git pull
   ↓
.site\public
   ↓
C:\xampp\htdocs\helvete\lab
   ↓
Internet
That is exactly the level of boring I wanted.
Naturally, the very last boss fight was SSL.
The certificate for helvete.pizza had expired and the old win-acme renewal had apparently been failing for a while.
It had:
247 errors

Cool.
Trying to renew it hit an ACME ARI replaces error, so I created a fresh certificate instead, used HTTP validation against the existing Apache root, exported new PEM files straight into Apache’s certificate directory, restarted Apache, and cleaned out the dead renewal.
Finally:
helvete.pizza/lab/
Shag’s Lab is live.
It is not really a blog.
It is not really a wiki.
It is not really a portfolio.
It is my project diary, and the website is just one way of looking at it.
If the website dies, I still have the vault.
If Quartz dies, I still have the vault.
If I redesign the whole thing later, I still have the vault.
If my PC dies, GitHub has the vault.
And if Future Me is staring at the smoking remains of all of this wondering what the hell Past Me did, I made him a Shag’s Lab - Doomsday Rebuild Guide.
You’re welcome, asshole.
Obsidian Vault to Website Home

updates/2026-09-20.1---cosmic-raven-reco.title: 2026-09-20.1 - Cosmic Raven Records
updates/2026-09-20.1---cosmic-raven-reco.content:
I Started An Interdimensional Record Label
Well, sort of.
This started because I have a pile of old music.
Not just finished songs. Half-finished songs. Demos. Ideas. Things I recorded twenty years ago and never really did anything with. Songs where I still remember what I wanted them to become even if I never actually got them there.
Then AI music tools got good enough that I could start feeding some of that stuff in and hearing completely different realizations of it.
That was weirdly emotional.
Not because I thought the AI had somehow resurrected my old band or uncovered the One True Version of a song. It was more like hearing a possibility I never got to hear the first time around.
What if I had arranged it differently?
What if somebody else had written that part?
What if I had actually finished the damn thing?
And then I had the thought that turned this from “Shawn makes AI covers of his old songs” into something much stupider and much more interesting.
What if the different versions were the point?
So I made a fictional record label.
Cosmic Raven Records.
The basic premise is that I accidentally built a weird homemade receiver. At first I just call it a radio because I have no better word for it.
Except it does not seem to tune into stations.
It tunes into possibilities.
At least that is what fictional me thinks is happening.
I can feed it a song I know, turn the dial, and somewhere in the static there is another version of it. Sometimes it is dramatically different. Sometimes it is almost the same except for a melody, a guitar sound, a vocal inflection, or one little decision that somehow changes the whole thing.
The important part is that I do not want the story to establish a giant hard-science cosmology where I explain exactly how alternate realities work.
The narrator is guessing.
Maybe it is alternate realities.
Maybe it is timelines.
Maybe it is possibilities.
Maybe the machine is doing something completely different and this idiot with a soldering iron has absolutely no idea.
That last one feels pretty believable.
I have been calling the whole thing a found-media music fiction project.
A slightly fancier version would be:

A transmedia fiction project built around music recovered from alternate realities.

It has some ARG DNA, but it is not really an ARG. Nobody has to solve a cipher to hear the next song. I am not trying to convince anyone that I genuinely have an interdimensional radio in my basement.
The fiction is the presentation.
Every song gets archived as a transmission.
 
TRANSMISSION 001A
 
TRANSMISSION 002A
 
TRANSMISSION 002B
 
TRANSMISSION 003A
 
...
 
The number is the underlying song, signal, or experiment.
The letter is another stable version I recovered.
That became useful almost immediately because I kept ending up with multiple versions of the same songs that I liked for completely different reasons.
Instead of choosing one and throwing the others away, now that indecision is canon.
Hell yes.
The first few transmissions are mostly fictional me having an existential crisis about the machine.
That part came pretty naturally because there is a real question underneath the fiction that I find interesting.
If I hear a musical idea generated from something I wrote, and then I take that idea back into my own music, whose idea is it now?
Is that inspiration?
Is it cheating?
If the fiction says another version of me wrote it, am I stealing from myself?
There is no big sermon or answer hidden in the project. I just think the question is interesting, so the narrator gets to wrestle with it too.
Then I started expanding the machine.
The original setup was just the radio and an input signal. I started calling the amount of original source being fed into it the Anchor. More source keeps the recovered version closer to what I know. Lower the Anchor and things start to drift.
Then fictional me decided hearing the signal was not enough and connected an old CRT television to the mess.
This was supposed to make the interference easier to see.
Naturally it made everything worse.
Controls on the television that should have absolutely nothing to do with the music started changing the music.
That gave me a few more homemade terms:
 
Anchor
 
Drift
 
Depth
 
Stability
 
They are not supposed to sound like official science terms. They are literally just words some guy writes in his notes because he needs names for the weird behaviors he keeps seeing.
That distinction matters to me.
I want the machine to grow along with the story instead of retroactively revealing that I secretly built the fucking TARDIS in Transmission 001.
It was a radio.
Then it was a radio with a TV connected to it.
Now he mostly calls the whole mess the receiver.
Eventually I want using it to become almost mundane.
That is actually one of my favorite parts of the idea.
Early on, every signal is impossible and terrifying.
Later I want fictional me saying shit like:

Stability was garbage so I backed the depth off and found it again twenty minutes later.

Like this is just what he does on a Tuesday now.
That also solves another problem I had.
A lot of the music I have made with AI is serious.
Some of it is absolutely not.
I have stupid songs. Comedy songs. Things that should not exist. Things that probably qualify as crimes against genre conventions.
At first I was worried that putting those next to the serious transmissions would wreck the tone.
Then I realized that is backwards.
If the receiver can find music from effectively anywhere, why would every reality have impeccable taste and a grim cinematic aesthetic?
Somewhere out there, somebody made the stupid song.
We found it.
We release what we find.
That is way more fun.
The newest part of the story is fictional me finally giving in and deciding to actually study the receiver instead of constantly whining that he needs to stop using it.
Transmission 005B is deliberately 005B.
There is no public 005A.
I am not explaining that yet.
Maybe I never will.
I like that the archive can have holes in it.
Transmission 006 starts getting more procedural. I have three versions of the same song, so the story is moving into a controlled repeatability test: same source, same settings, same process, and somehow the receiver still does not quite return to the same place.
That gives me 006A, 006B, and 006C without having to pretend each version is a completely separate event.
The YouTube presentation has become its own little project too.
I wrote a Windows BAT file around FFmpeg that turns a WAV into the full transmission video and thumbnail.
The command is basically:
 
make_transmission.v4.bat "Song.wav" "006A" "Artist Name" "Track Name"
 
It builds a five-second acquisition intro, stitches the intro audio and song together, draws the Cosmic Raven HUD, generates an audio spectrum, adds transmission metadata, renders the MP4, then creates a YouTube thumbnail.
The current videos are intentionally a little sterile and broadcast-y. Static background, HUD, signal status, visualizer, archive metadata.
I already want to redesign it.
I also absolutely do not want to redesign it right now.
Those are both true.
There were, naturally, a bunch of dumb little Windows and FFmpeg problems along the way.
Parentheses in filenames taught me exciting new things about CMD parsing.
FFmpeg taught me that colons are apparently dangerous.
A receiver timer taught me that sometimes the right feature is the one you delete.
And native FFmpeg progress output taught me that I would rather parse its machine-readable progress with PowerShell than watch Windows Terminal fill itself with twenty-seven wrapped copies of the same status line.
Eventually the generator reached the magical software-development milestone known as:

Okay, quit fucking touching it for a minute. It works.

So naturally I have now put the code under Git and written a full doomsday rebuild guide.
The rebuild notes cover the folder structure, FFmpeg installation, exact asset names, the audio-stitching pipeline, the thumbnail generator, the visualizer settings, the Windows BAT landmines, transmission numbering, and the narrative rules I am likely to forget.
Because I know myself.
Five years from now I will absolutely open this folder and say:

What the fuck is .crr_combined_audio.wav

Now Future Me has documentation.
You are welcome, asshole.
The actual story text lives in a Google Doc called Cosmic Raven Records - Transmission Script.
That has turned out to be really useful because I can treat it as the single source of truth for descriptions and drafts instead of having slightly different copies scattered through chats, text files, and YouTube.
Pinned comments have also become part of the format.
I originally thought of them as teasers for the next transmission, but I like them much better as later annotations.
The description is what fictional me believed when he archived the signal.
A pinned comment added later can say, basically:

I went back through my notes. I was wrong about this.

That means the old posts can continue participating in the story without rewriting history every time I come up with a better explanation.
I am being very explicit outside the fiction that this uses AI.
Every transmission includes this:

About Cosmic Raven Records:  


This is a fictional music and worldbuilding project using a mix of human-created and AI-generated music, visuals, writing, direction, editing, and curation. The transmissions, artists, histories, and alternate realities are part of the fiction.


This is all an experiment.

I do not think hiding the tools would make the project more interesting.
The fun part is what I am doing with them.
So that is Cosmic Raven Records so far.
A fake interdimensional record label.
A music archive.
A story told through YouTube descriptions and comments.
A pile of old songs getting strange second lives.
A growing collection of fictional artists and realities I have not even gotten to yet.
And one increasingly comfortable idiot sitting in front of a radio and an old television, turning the dial to see what else is out there.
There are a bunch of obvious next steps.
The video presentation could use more motion and better backgrounds. I want genre metadata. I want a better archive system as the catalogue grows. Eventually I want to figure out Shorts that feel like actual recovered signal fragments instead of advertisements for the full videos.
But I am deliberately not disappearing into infrastructure right now.
The machine works.
I have songs to release.
So I am going to keep turning the dial.
